summary.text: Lucas congruences pair the low and high summands to show all entries with index at least \(p\) vanish modulo \(p\); at index \(p-1\), an alternating geometric sum gives \(1\) in the first case, while divisibility of the central binomial factors leaves only the midpoint, giving \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\), in the second. Thus both Hankel matrices are anti-triangular modulo \(p\), and multiplying the powers of their constant anti-diagonal entries by the reversal-permutation sign \((-1)^{(p-1)/2}\) yields the two claimed residues.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^4
\]
and
\[
c(n)=\sum_{k=0}^n(-1)^k\binom nk^2\binom{2k}{k}
                  \binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.
\]
Fix an odd prime \(p\), and put
\[
m=\frac{p-1}{2}.
\]
All calculations until the final paragraph will be in the field \(\mathbb F_p\). We write equality in this field simply as \(=\), so that each such equality is a congruence modulo \(p\) for the corresponding integers.

We first record the binomial-coefficient facts that will be used. Lucas's congruence, in the one-digit form needed here, says
\[
 \binom nk\equiv
 \binom{n\bmod p}{k\bmod p}
 \binom{\lfloor n/p\rfloor}{\lfloor k/p\rfloor}\pmod p.
\tag{1}
\]
This follows, for example, by comparing coefficients in
\((1+x)^p\equiv 1+x^p\pmod p\), and then iterating according to the base-\(p\) digits. We use the usual convention that \(\binom uv=0\) when \(v>u\).

For \(0\le k<p\), we also have
\[
 \binom{p-1}{k}=(-1)^k.
\tag{2}
\]
Indeed, starting with \(\binom{p-1}{0}=1\), the recurrence
\[
 (k+1)\binom{p-1}{k+1}=(p-1-k)\binom{p-1}{k}
\]
gives the result inductively, since \(k+1\) is nonzero and hence invertible modulo \(p\), while \(p-1-k=-(k+1)\) in \(\mathbb F_p\).

Now let \(0\le r<p\). Applying (1) gives the following three useful formulas. If \(0\le k<p\), then
\[
 \binom{p+r}{k}=\binom rk.
\tag{3}
\]
Consequently this coefficient is zero when \(r<k<p\). If \(0\le l<p\), then
\[
 \binom{p+r}{p+l}=\binom rl.
\tag{4}
\]
In particular, when \(0\le l\le r\), the coefficients in (3) at \(k=l\) and in (4) at \(k=p+l\) are equal modulo \(p\).

We will also need two facts about central binomial coefficients. Set
\[
 Q_t=\binom{2t}{t}.
\]
If \(0\le t<p\) and \(p\le 2t\), then
\[
 Q_t=0.
\tag{5}
\]
To see this, write \(2t=p+(2t-p)\). The lower base-\(p\) digit of the top is \(2t-p<t\), whereas the lower digit of the bottom is \(t\). Lucas's congruence therefore contains the zero factor \(\binom{2t-p}{t}\).

For every \(0\le t<p\), one further has
\[
 Q_{p+t}=2Q_t.
\tag{6}
\]
There are two cases. If \(2t<p\), the base-\(p\) digits of \(2(p+t)\) are \((2,2t)\), while those of \(p+t\) are \((1,t)\). Thus Lucas's congruence gives
\[
 \binom{2(p+t)}{p+t}
 =\binom21\binom{2t}{t}=2Q_t.
\]
If \(2t\ge p\), then the right side is zero by (5). On the left, the lower base-\(p\) digits are respectively \(2t-p\) and \(t\), and \(2t-p<t\), so Lucas's congruence also makes the left side zero. This proves (6) in all cases.

We next determine the entries of the two Hankel matrices on and beyond their antidiagonals.

First consider \(a(p+r)\), where
\[
0\le r\le p-2.
\]
Split its defining sum into the three ranges
\[
0\le k\le r,\qquad r<k<p,\qquad p\le k\le p+r.
\]
For the middle range, (3) gives \(\binom{p+r}{k}=0\), so every middle summand is zero modulo \(p\).

In the last range write \(k=p+l\), where \(0\le l\le r\). Since \(p\) is odd,
\[
 (-1)^{p+l}=-(-1)^l.
\]
Moreover, (3) and (4) give
\[
 \binom{p+r}{p+l}=\binom rl=\binom{p+r}{l}.
\]
It follows that the summand indexed by \(p+l\) is the negative of the summand indexed by \(l\):
\[
 (-1)^{p+l}\binom{p+r}{p+l}^4
 =-(-1)^l\binom{p+r}{l}^4.
\]
Thus the low and high ranges cancel term by term, and hence
\[
 a(p+r)=0\qquad(0\le r\le p-2).
\tag{7}
\]

At the preceding index \(p-1\), formula (2) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a(p-1)
 &=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\binom{p-1}{k}^4\\
 &=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\bigl((-1)^k\bigr)^4\\
 &=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k.
\end{aligned}
\]
There are an odd number \(p\) of terms in this alternating sum, beginning and ending with \(1\), so
\[
 a(p-1)=1.
\tag{8}
\]

We now establish the corresponding statements for \(c\). Again let \(0\le r\le p-2\), set \(n=p+r\), and split the defining sum for \(c(n)\) into the same three ranges. For \(r<k<p\), the factor \(\binom{p+r}{k}^2\) is zero by (3), so the middle range contributes zero.

It remains to pair the term indexed by \(l\), for \(0\le l\le r\), with that indexed by \(p+l\). For the low index \(l\), note that
\[
n-l=p+r-l=p+(r-l).
\]
Using (3) and (6), its summand is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(-1)^l\binom{p+r}{l}^2Q_lQ_{p+r-l}\\
&\qquad=(-1)^l\binom rl^2Q_l\bigl(2Q_{r-l}\bigr)\\
&\qquad=2(-1)^l\binom rl^2Q_lQ_{r-l}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}
\]
For the high index \(p+l\), we have
\[
n-(p+l)=r-l.
\]
Using (4), (6), and the oddness of \(p\), its summand is
\[
\begin{aligned}
&(-1)^{p+l}\binom{p+r}{p+l}^2Q_{p+l}Q_{r-l}\\
&\qquad=-(-1)^l\binom rl^2\bigl(2Q_l\bigr)Q_{r-l}\\
&\qquad=-2(-1)^l\binom rl^2Q_lQ_{r-l}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
Equations (9) and (10) show that these two terms cancel. Therefore
\[
 c(p+r)=0\qquad(0\le r\le p-2).
\tag{11}
\]

It remains to evaluate \(c(p-1)\). Recall that \(p-1=2m\). Consider the summand indexed by \(k\), where \(0\le k<p\). If \(k<m\), put \(t=p-1-k\). Then \(t<p\), and
\[
2t=2(p-1-k)\ge p,
\]
because \(k<m=(p-1)/2\). Thus (5) shows that the right-hand central binomial factor
\[
\binom{2(p-1-k)}{p-1-k}=Q_t
\]
is zero. If \(k>m\), then \(k<p\) and \(2k\ge p\), so (5) shows that the left-hand central binomial factor \(Q_k\) is zero. Hence every term except the one with \(k=m\) vanishes modulo \(p\).

For \(k=m\), both \(k\) and \((p-1)-k\) equal \(m\), and \(2m=p-1\). Thus the surviving term is
\[
 (-1)^m\binom{p-1}{m}^2
 \binom{p-1}{m}\binom{p-1}{m}.
\]
By (2), \(\binom{p-1}{m}=(-1)^m\). Its square is therefore \(1\), so both the squared binomial factor and the product of the two central binomial factors are \(1\). Consequently
\[
 c(p-1)=(-1)^m.
\tag{12}
\]

We now apply these entrywise congruences to the determinants. Work first over \(\mathbb F_p\), and let
\[
\overline A_{ij}=a(i+j),\qquad
\overline C_{ij}=c(i+j),
\qquad 0\le i,j<p,
\]
where the entries are reduced modulo \(p\).

We use the following elementary determinant observation. Suppose a \(p\times p\) matrix \(M\) satisfies
\[
 M_{ij}=0\quad\text{if }i+j\ge p,
\]
and
\[
 M_{ij}=d\quad\text{if }i+j=p-1.
\]
Reverse the order of its rows. The resulting matrix \(B\) has
\[
 B_{ij}=M_{p-1-i,j}.
\]
If \(j>i\), then \((p-1-i)+j\ge p\), so \(B_{ij}=0\). On the diagonal,
\[
 B_{ii}=M_{p-1-i,i}=d.
\]
Thus \(B\) is triangular with every diagonal entry equal to \(d\), and
\[
 \det B=d^p.
\]
The row-reversal permutation has one inversion for every pair of distinct rows, hence \(p(p-1)/2\) inversions and sign
\[
 s=(-1)^{p(p-1)/2}.
\]
Since \(\det B=s\det M\), and \(s^{-1}=s\), we obtain
\[
 \det M=s\,d^p.
\tag{13}
\]
Because \(p=2m+1\),
\[
\frac{p(p-1)}2=pm,
\]
and \(p\) is odd. Therefore
\[
 s=(-1)^{pm}=(-1)^m.
\tag{14}
\]

For \(\overline A\), if \(i+j\ge p\), then \(i+j=p+r\) for some \(0\le r\le p-2\), since \(i,j\le p-1\). Equation (7) therefore makes that entry zero. Equation (8) says that every antidiagonal entry, for which \(i+j=p-1\), equals \(1\). Applying (13) with \(d=1\), and then (14), gives
\[
 \det\overline A=(-1)^m\cdot 1^p=(-1)^m.
\tag{15}
\]

For \(\overline C\), equation (11) likewise makes every entry with \(i+j\ge p\) zero, while (12) says that every antidiagonal entry equals \((-1)^m\). Thus (13) and (14) give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \det\overline C
 &=(-1)^m\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(p\) is odd, \(\bigl((-1)^m\bigr)^p=(-1)^m\). Hence
\[
 \det\overline C=(-1)^m(-1)^m=1.
\tag{16}
\]

Finally, reducing an integer matrix entrywise modulo \(p\) commutes with taking its determinant, because the determinant is a sum of signed products of entries. Therefore \(\det\overline A\) and \(\det\overline C\) are respectively the reductions modulo \(p\) of the two original integer determinants. Equations (15) and (16), with \(m=(p-1)/2\), prove
\[
\det(a(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv(-1)^{(p-1)/2}\pmod p
\]
and
\[
\det(c(i+j))_{0\le i,j<p}\equiv1\pmod p.
\]
This establishes both asserted congruences.
